questions.question: Young women painted glowing numbers on watch dials for the United States Radium Corporation in New Jersey. Its supervisors had them shape their brushes to a fine point with their lips, and the company told them the radium paint was harmless. With every lick the women swallowed a trace of radium. Years later the radium was still inside them, giving off radiation. Why had their bodies kept it?
questions.answer: They built it into bone, as they do calcium
choices: They built it into bone, as they do calcium
They built it into red blood cells, as they do iron
They gathered it in the thyroid, as they do iodine
They held it in muscle cells, as they do potassium
questions.context: Radium sits in the same column of the periodic table as calcium, and the body handles the two alike, laying radium down in bone, where its alpha particles strike the living cells nearby year after year; radium-226 takes about 1,600 years to decay by half. The thyroid does gather iodine and muscle cells hold most of the body's potassium, but radium follows calcium. Studies of the painters gave the first safety limit for radium held in a worker's body, and the Manhattan Project's doctors set their first limit for plutonium by comparing plutonium with radium.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade teaches that the elements in one group of the periodic table share properties (TEKS 2017 8.5C); radium follows its group-mate calcium into bone.

questions.question: Arthur Roeder, president of the United States Radium Corporation, asked Cecil Drinker of the Harvard School of Public Health to study the company's dial-painting plant in New Jersey. Drinker found the plant saturated with radium dust, and his report judged that radium was making the women who painted the dials ill. Roeder insisted that an infection caught outside the factory was to blame. What did the company send New Jersey's Department of Labor?
questions.answer: Drinker's report, changed to say all were well
choices: Drinker's report, changed to say all were well
Drinker's report, just as he had written it
Drinker's report, changed to blame an infection
Nothing, for Roeder kept the report back
questions.context: Alice Hamilton, a Harvard expert on poisons at work, learned that the state's copy said 'every girl is in perfect condition', and in 1925 she asked Katherine Drinker whether Roeder could have issued 'a forged report in your name'. The Drinkers then published their real findings, though Roeder had threatened to sue and had never shown them the company report he said refuted them.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to its impact on society (TEKS 2021 8.4A); Drinker's study is evidence that a company was handed and altered.

questions.question: Chemie Grünenthal began selling thalidomide as a sleeping pill in West Germany in 1957, at first with no prescription needed, and its advertising called the drug non-toxic. On what evidence did the company rest that claim?
questions.answer: Rats and mice had survived huge doses
choices: Rats and mice had survived huge doses
Monkeys given it for months stayed well
Pregnant animals given it had healthy young
Many pregnant women had taken it safely
questions.context: Grünenthal's rodent tests found no dose that would kill, and tests on rodents alone were usual at the time. No pregnant animals were tested and the drug was never tried in pregnant women, though doctors gave it for morning sickness, and rats and mice later proved far less sensitive than rabbits and some monkeys to its harm to unborn young. Late in 1961 Widukind Lenz and William McBride linked it to babies born with shortened or missing limbs, and Grünenthal withdrew it.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to society and the process of science (TEKS 2021 8.4A); a test that found no deaths did not show the drug was safe.

questions.question: Frances Kelsey joined the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in August 1960, and one of her first files was Richardson-Merrell's application to sell thalidomide in America. She refused to approve it, month after month, while the company pressed her. What was her objection when she first sent it back, in November 1960?
questions.answer: It had not been shown to be safe
choices: It had not been shown to be safe
It had already harmed babies in Europe
It had killed patients who took too many
It had made patients depend on it
questions.context: Kelsey judged that the file leaned on doctors' praise in place of clinical data, with shaky figures on how the body absorbs the drug and unfinished animal studies, and she insisted on hard evidence of safety. She knew of no harm to babies: that link was found in Europe about a year later. The law of the day let the FDA refuse a drug not shown to be safe, but an application took effect by itself after 60 days unless the agency acted, so she sent it back again and again for more data.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to society and the process of science (TEKS 2021 8.4A); Kelsey's demand for evidence of safety is the method at work.

questions.question: Frances Kelsey was still holding back thalidomide at the US Food and Drug Administration when a Scottish doctor, A. Leslie Florence, wrote to the British Medical Journal. Four of his patients, on the sleeping pill nightly for over a year, had numb, tingling hands and feet, signs of nerve damage. Kelsey then asked the drug's maker for proof that it could not harm a baby before birth. Why did his report make her ask that?
questions.answer: Her own tests had shown some drugs reach the unborn
choices: Her own tests had shown some drugs reach the unborn
Its maker had said the drug reached the unborn
Nerve damage in a parent passes on through the genes
Doctors in Europe had already tied it to birth defects
questions.context: The report sent Kelsey back to her own wartime research on drugs for malaria, which had shown that some drugs pass through the placenta from a mother to her unborn young, and she doubted the maker's unsupported claim that thalidomide did not. Doctors did not link the drug to birth defects until late in 1961. Its maker, Richardson-Merrell, withdrew its application in March 1962.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to society and the process of science (TEKS 2021 8.4A); Kelsey joined an odd side effect to what her own research showed of drugs and the unborn, and asked for evidence (map line G8.M3).

questions.question: Frances Kelsey had worked under a law of 1938 that asked a drug company to show only that a new drug was safe. Once thalidomide's harm in Europe came to light, Congress passed the Kefauver-Harris Amendments in October 1962, which added a second thing a company must show before it sells a new drug. What was it?
questions.answer: Controlled studies showing it works as claimed
choices: Controlled studies showing it works as claimed
Controlled studies showing it beats older drugs
Controlled studies showing it cures the illness
Controlled studies showing it works in every patient
questions.context: The law asks for 'substantial evidence' of the effect a drug claims, drawn from 'adequate and well-controlled investigations'; it does not ask that a drug cure, beat older drugs or work in every patient, since not everyone responds to a medicine the same way. It also required that patients in drug trials give informed consent and that makers report side effects. The economist Sam Peltzman argued in 1973 that the new rules also sharply cut the number of new drugs reaching patients each year, a cost the law's defenders weigh against the harms it prevents.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to society, including cost-benefit analysis (TEKS 2021 8.4A); the 1962 law made evidence that a drug works a condition of sale.

questions.question: Doctors of the US Public Health Service began a study in Macon County, Alabama, in 1932 with about 600 Black men: about 400 had syphilis, and about 200 did not. The men were told they were being treated for 'bad blood', a local term for many ills, and were given free medical exams and hot meals. What did the doctors set out to learn?
questions.answer: What syphilis does when left untreated
choices: What syphilis does when left untreated
What a new drug could do against syphilis
Whether healthy men given syphilis would fall ill
Whether a vaccine could prevent syphilis
questions.context: The Public Health Service meant to record the natural course of syphilis left untreated, in a study planned at first to last six to eight months and soon stretched to follow the men for the rest of their lives. Its doctors argued that the knowledge would help fight the disease, at a time when the treatments, compounds of arsenic and mercury, were toxic and only mildly effective; but the men were never told they had syphilis and never asked for their informed consent. The doctors did not give anyone the disease: the 399 already had it when they were enrolled.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to its impact on society (TEKS 2021 8.4A); the study is the classic case for why research on people needs consent.

questions.question: Penicillin had become the standard cure for syphilis by the late 1940s. The US Public Health Service study in Macon County, Alabama, still followed hundreds of men who had the disease. What did the study's doctors do about the new cure?
questions.answer: They did not offer it to the men
choices: They did not offer it to the men
They gave it to every man who had syphilis
They gave it to half the sick men, to compare
They offered it, but most of the men refused
questions.context: The men were not offered penicillin, and the Public Health Service had already worked to keep them from treatment elsewhere, giving local doctors lists of the men in 1934 and keeping them from treatment when they were drafted in the Second World War. The study was no secret: its doctors published reports on the men in medical journals for decades. Some of the men's wives caught the disease, and some of their children were born with it.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to its impact on society (TEKS 2021 8.4A); the cure withheld is the turning point of the Tuskegee record.

questions.question: Peter Buxtun, who interviewed patients with sexually transmitted diseases for the US Public Health Service in San Francisco, protested its Alabama syphilis study to his superiors in 1966 and again in 1968. A committee of the Public Health Service reviewed the study in 1969 and let it go on. What brought the study to an end in 1972?
questions.answer: A news story carried across the nation
choices: A news story carried across the nation
A court order won by the men's lawyers
A new law passed by the US Congress
The death of the last man in the study
questions.context: The 1969 committee saw a unique chance to study late syphilis. Buxtun then passed his papers to the Associated Press, and its reporter Jean Heller broke the story on 25 July 1972; an advisory panel judged the study 'ethically unjustified', and it was ended on 16 November 1972, with 74 of the men still alive. The men's lawsuit and the new law for research came afterwards.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to its impact on society (TEKS 2021 8.4A); Buxtun's years of protest are dissent inside an institution.

questions.question: Congress passed the National Research Act in answer to the US Public Health Service's study of syphilis in Alabama. Under the federal rules that grew from it, most research on people that the US government pays for needs approval before it begins. What must approve it?
questions.answer: A review board that includes a non-scientist
choices: A review board that includes a non-scientist
A review board made up only of senior scientists
A review board inside the Surgeon General's office
A review board of judges from the federal courts
questions.context: Such a board, an institutional review board (IRB), must have at least one member whose concerns lie outside science and one from outside the institution; it weighs the risks to the people in a study and checks that each gives informed consent: told the truth, understanding it, and free to say no. The commission the act set up wrote the Belmont Report, finished in 1978 and published in 1979, whose principles are respect for persons, beneficence and justice.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to its impact on society (TEKS 2021 8.4A); society, not science, decided the rules for research on people (map line G8.M3).

27278cb863.why: Judge medium (stance): the stem named no one; it now names the United States Radium Corporation, whose supervisors had the painters point their brushes with their lips and which told them the paint was harmless (F2, F39). Illinois and the loose 'from about 1917' are gone (judge low, fact). Judge low (tell): radium and calcium were the only '-ium' pair; the vitamins lure is now 'muscle cells, as they do potassium' (F40), so two choices end in '-ium'. The card drops 'fell ill' and takes the dropped 7dcdd22bd0's lesson in one sentence (the first limit for radium in the body; the plutonium limit by comparison, F10, F11), without naming who chaired the committee. Key unchanged.

ea6f835067.why: Judge low (clarity): 'the women' arrived unintroduced and the key's 'all' had no clear referent; the stem now says 'the women who painted the dials', so 'all were well' plainly means them. Key, choices and card unchanged.

ac5ccbf81a.why: Fact-check error: the card said Kelsey could refuse only by proving the drug unsafe. The 1938 law let the FDA refuse a drug not shown to be safe; the catch was that an application took effect by itself after 60 days unless the agency acted (Weinberger v. Hynson; Science History Institute; F34). The card now says so, and agrees with her 'burden of proof' line on 00cf2f4370's card; the key, 'not shown to be safe', already fits. Judge low: the lure 'It had failed to help patients sleep' was killed by 25ebd2a5ce's stem (the 1938 law asked only for safety); it is now 'It had made patients depend on it' (thalidomide was sold on its low addiction potential, and dependence is not among her recorded grounds, F36, F18). Stem unchanged.

17be8bd269.why: Judge medium (tell): the key, proof of safety for unborn babies, was thalidomide's headline. The stem now states that request and asks why a report of nerve damage led her to it, so her reasoning decides: her own wartime research had shown some drugs pass the placenta (F35: Wikipedia, Grokipedia, UChicago). The headline now points to a wrong choice, the M1 timing myth (doctors in Europe tied it to birth defects only late in 1961, F14); the other lures are the maker's claim reversed (it said the drug did not cross the placenta, F19) and the heredity mistake (acquired damage is not passed on in the genes, F37). No lure is the only one about the letter. 'The company' is now 'the maker', introduced. The 'better than older pills' lure that 25ebd2a5ce's stem killed is gone.

25ebd2a5ce.why: Judge medium (tell): two lures were dead (approval abroad, against a drug that harmed babies where it was approved; a cost test) and the key alone carried a mark of quality. All four choices now begin 'Controlled studies showing it', so the content decides: works as claimed (key; 21 U.S.C. 355(d), F22), beats older drugs (M3), cures the illness, works in every patient (each believable, none asked by the law, F22, F38; not everyone responds to a medicine the same way, NHGRI). 'Has no side effects' was not used: beside the stem's 'only that a new drug was safe' it reads as the first thing, not a second. No lure is 'doctors' praise', which ac5ccbf81a's card would have killed. The card now says what the law does not ask. Stem unchanged.

026cc989e2.why: Fact-check uncertain: the study was planned at first to last six to eight months, then extended indefinitely (ASU Embryo Project, F41), so the key 'if it is never treated' and the card's lifelong plan were wrong for 1932. The key is now 'when left untreated' (true of the first plan and the extension; CDC: 'the natural history of untreated syphilis') and the card says it was planned for six to eight months and soon stretched. Judge low: 'men given syphilis would get well' was dead beside a stem that says 400 had it; the lure is now 'Whether healthy men given syphilis would fall ill', which the 200 healthy men keep live and the card refutes (M4). One lure now opens 'What' so the key is not the only 'What' choice. Stem unchanged.

7d2b959afb.why: Fact-check uncertain and judge low: 'Dozens of the men died' understated the usual figures (28 of syphilis, about 100 of its complications) and made a second harm clause. The deaths are left out; the one harm clause is the sourced wives-and-children line, now exact (wives caught it; children were born with it, F31). Stem, key and choices unchanged.

2b31e6cc92.why: Fact-check error: the 1969 agency was the National Communicable Disease Center (a bureau of the US Public Health Service; renamed Center for Disease Control only in 1970, F42); the stem now says 'a committee of the Public Health Service'. Fact-check uncertain: Buxtun reached Jean Heller through the AP's Edith Lederer; the card now says he passed his papers to the Associated Press and Heller broke the story (F43). Judge low: the key 'made it public' clashed with 7d2b959afb's card (the study was published in journals); it is now 'A news story carried across the nation'. Judge low: 'venereal' is now 'sexually transmitted'.

a275e0d12a.why: Judge medium (tell): the key alone was a body with a stated purpose; all four are now review boards, told apart by who sits on them or where they sit, and the key states the rule (45 CFR 46.107: at least one member whose concerns are nonscientific, F45) against its opposite, a board of scientists only. Judge medium (leak): 'after the study came to light' handed 033edf1190 its key and '1974' killed its law lure; the stem now says only 'in answer to' the study, with no year, and the card names none. Fact-check error: the Belmont Report was finished in 1978 and published in 1979 (F44); the card says so. Fact-check note: 'nearly all' is now 'most' (exempt categories).

dropped.question: Grace Fryer and four other New Jersey dial painters won a settlement from the United States Radium Corporation in 1928, and Catherine Donohue won her case against the Radium Dial Company in Illinois in 1938. Robley Evans, a physicist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, studied former dial painters in the 1930s. A committee he chaired set the first 'tolerance level' for radium workers in 1941. What did it cap?
dropped.why: Judge high (grade): the 1941 tolerance level is a health-physics footnote, not 8th-grade content, and its only grade-fit idea (radium stays in the body) is 42ec043e2c's; the lead agreed. Fact-check error dropped with it: L. F. Curtiss, not Robley Evans, chaired the National Bureau of Standards committee. The card's lesson (the first limit for radium in the body; the plutonium limit set by comparison) moved to 42ec043e2c's card without the chair.

lead_edits.old: In May 1961 she wrote to its maker, Richardson-Merrell, that 'the burden of proof that the drug is safe' lay with the applicant, and the company withdrew its application in March 1962.
lead_edits.new: Its maker, Richardson-Merrell, withdrew its application in March 1962.
